1:
The refusal to name a date is read as a diagnosis of the appetite behind the question. Chrysostom says nothing is so prone to pry into things obscure as the nature of men, and that this happens when the mind is unsettled and idle; children never cease teasing their nurses with when will this be and when that, and the apostles themselves asked twice, before the Passion and after the Resurrection, and asked nothing sooner. Calvin turns it into a purpose: it is excessive incredulity not to believe what the Lord foretells unless he marks the day out as it were with the finger, and Christ designed that the day should be hid from us, that being in suspense we might be as it were upon watch. Henry draws the practical line, that there are times and seasons for us to do our work in, but the time when we must give up our account we know not, nor is it needful. Ellicott calls the phrase a Hebraism in which the second word is the more explicit, so that we should say about day and hour, and takes the plural for the various periods at which men might think the advent likely; Robertson separates them, the one an extended period, the other a definite space of time.

Clarke alone reads the passage of another judgment. He couples the destruction of Jerusalem with the final assize, holds that Paul speaks here chiefly of the former, and appeals to his own note on the same two words in Acts, where he referred them to the fall of the Jewish commonwealth. The cry of peace and safety he takes for the state of the Jewish people when the Romans came against them, so persuaded God would not deliver the city and temple to their enemies that they refused every overture; and the sudden destruction is the storming of the city, the burning of the temple, the massacre of hundreds of thousands, the rest sold for slaves and dispersed over the earth. Everyone else takes the day of the Lord as the return to judgment, Ellicott noting that the phrase is drawn from the Old Testament, where it means not primarily the last judgment but any set time God has fixed for a visitation, the plague of locusts in Joel, or vengeance on the heathen, widening in Isaiah into a general day for mankind.

The paradox in know perfectly is caught by two. Ellicott calls it an oxymoron: I need not tell you about the time, for you know to a nicety not the hour of Christ's coming but the utter uncertainty respecting it. Robertson puts it the same way, that what they accurately know is their own ignorance. Ellicott adds that the frequency of the thief simile shows it was the ordinary formula in which the doctrine was taught. Barnes presses the comparison: a thief gives no warning and is careful that none shall be given, which proves every attempt to fix the year or the century fallacious, for if men could ascertain it the coming would not be like a thief at all. On the travail Ellicott quotes an ancient comment that the woman knows she has the child to bear but not the time of her pangs, then objects that it hardly suits here, since those on whom the destruction bursts live in no expectation of judgment. Calvin finds the aptness elsewhere, that a woman carries in her womb the occasion of grief without feeling it until she is seized amidst feasting or in sleep, and traces the sleep of the wicked to a deep contempt of God. Barnes takes destruction to mean not annihilation but the pulling down of what a thing is, and asks whether being destroyed and being saved can be the same. Gill marks only that the speakers are men in a state of unregeneracy.
4:
What the darkness is gets defined narrowly. Ellicott says the words are suggested by the mention of night and that the chief thought is supineness and torpor, not so much ignorance or sin, and that the day is so called because it is a day indeed and not merely a point of time. Wesley compresses it to sleeping secure in sin, and Gill takes the darkness for the state of unregeneracy in which men are born, brought up and willingly walk. Clarke alone brings outside evidence, a maxim from the Midrash on the Psalms that God will judge the Gentiles in the night season, when they are asleep in their transgressions, but the Israelites in the day time, when they are occupied in the study of the law; he thinks the apostle has this notion in view through five verses together. There is also a variant here that two of them report: Ellicott notes that two of the best manuscripts and the Coptic, with Lachmann and Lightfoot, read as thieves rather than as a thief, but holds the received text better supported and better suited to a context about inadvertence rather than evil practices; Robertson names the same witnesses and says the reading turns the metaphor round.

On children of light the best note is Ellicott's. The expression is an enthusiastic Hebrew poetical turn for intimate vital connection with a thing, as children of this world means mere products of this age; children of light are therefore persons to whom darkness is alien, who have an intuitive responsiveness to whatever may be called light, and to such the day can never come as a startling apparition. He adds that Paul recognises no exceptions among the members of the Church, that the following exhortation shows it was a matter of each man's free will whether he sustained the character, and that the shift from ye to we is a courtesy. Barnes and Robertson both call the phrase a Hebraism, Robertson on the authority of Deissmann. Calvin sees Isaiah accomplished, that while darkness covers the earth the Lord arises upon us, and says it were unseemly to be caught by Christ asleep while the full blaze of light shines upon us. Clarke makes the light that of the dispensation itself, in which all the preceding dispensations have become luminous.

That the sleep and the drunkenness are figures is stated most plainly by Calvin: he does not mean natural sleep or drunkenness from wine, but stupor of mind, when, forgetting God and ourselves, we regardlessly indulge our vices; and spiritual sobriety is using this world so sparingly that we are not entangled with its allurements. Henry ties the two duties together, that while we are compassed with so many temptations to excess we shall not keep sober unless we are on our guard, and shall not long watch unless we keep sober. Barnes traces the verb, which means properly to be temperate in respect of wine and then to be sober-minded, and turns it into an examination: no votary of the world would wish to be summoned to the judgment bar from the theatre or the ballroom, but would ask a little time to prepare, so why not be habitually sober-minded, since the event may occur at any moment. The shame of daylight drunkenness is common ground. Barnes says that among the ancients daytime drunkenness was the greatest disgrace and cites two classical witnesses; Clarke calls it doubly scandalous even among the heathen; Ellicott observes that the streets even of heathen Thessalonica seldom showed drunken men by daylight, and adds that in Cyprian's time Christians were known from other men because their breath smelt of wine in the early morning, from attending the Sacrament, no heathen having touched wine by that hour. Robertson notes only that night was the favourite time for drunken revelries.
8:
Two of them warn against pressing the armour. Calvin says it is in vain that some seek a more refined exposition of the names of the kinds of armour, since Paul speaks here differently from Ephesians, and that though only two pieces are named nothing is omitted, for the man provided with faith, love and hope will be found in no department unarmed; his point is that the life of Christians is a perpetual warfare, and he adds that men intemperate in other situations refrain from every bodily delight when the enemy is near, so we should be at least as vigilant as soldiers are. Ellicott says the same more cautiously, that it seems far-fetched to make faith and love keep the heart and hope preserve the brain from miscalculating the danger, and notes that in Ephesians the cuirass is righteousness, faith becomes the shield, and love disappears from the panoply altogether; here the soldier is not aggressive but defensive, and the Christian is not only the porter sitting up to let his Lord in but the sentry liable to be surprised. Clarke maps the pieces anyway: faith enables us to endure as seeing him who is invisible, love makes us bear our troubles pleasantly, hope anticipates the glory that shall be revealed. Robertson traces the helmet to a late word found in Polybius and the papyri, and both he and Barnes send the reader to Isaiah.

Then comes the hardest verse in the chapter, and the division is sharp. Gill reads it as it stands: there are some who are vessels of wrath, fitted for destruction, of old ordained to condemnation, and it is distinguishing grace that we who equally deserved it are not appointed to it. Clarke attacks that head on. He grants that some were appointed to wrath and asks who, when and why, and answers that they are the Jews as a nation, appointed not from eternity but from the moment they finally rejected the gospel, which is why the apostles were told to begin at Jerusalem; and he insists that even this appointment does not signify eternal damnation, since many may have turned to the Lord who smote them during the siege. Wesley glosses the wrath in one line, as appointed to the obstinately impenitent. Ellicott refers the appointment to some mysterious moment of God's eternal counsels and adds that we ourselves are the only persons who can defeat God's predestinations; he presses the word rendered obtain to mean acquire by one's own efforts, and concludes that God does not predestinate men to salvation without laborious acquisition on their part, though the price can be paid only through union with Christ. Calvin takes the same word the other way: Paul does not mean that God has called us that we may procure salvation for ourselves, but that we may obtain what has been acquired for us by Christ. Barnes turns the verse into encouragement, illustrating it from the ancients consulting the flight of birds and the entrails of animals to learn whether the gods favoured them, whereas we learn it from the word.

On waking and sleeping the majority take life and death, Barnes adding that the point is that neither class has any advantage over the other, and Clarke that in either state believers have life and communion with him. Calvin alone hesitates, allowing that ordinary sleep might be meant. The closing word is ambiguous in the same way as at the end of the previous chapter, and Gill, Henry, Barnes and Calvin all note that it may be rendered comfort or exhort. Ellicott takes the building metaphor seriously, that each believer is himself a temple in continual process of completion, and Robertson unpacks the odd construction as build ye, one the one.
12:
Chrysostom begins from the difficulty of the office. A ruler must have many occasions of enmity: physicians trouble the sick and fathers annoy their children, yet the physician keeps the friends on his side and the father rules by nature and law, while the priest must rule men who are willing and thankful, which cannot soon come to pass, for whoever is reproved ceases to be thankful and becomes an enemy; and a man excluded from the prayers grieves not at the loss but at the public disgrace. Calvin makes the same point from the other end, that where the kingdom of God is lightly esteemed contempt of pious teachers follows; but he turns the titles into a test, since labour excludes all idle bellies from the number of pastors and instruction excludes those who glory in the name without teaching. He adds that judgment is committed to the Church to distinguish true pastors, for these marks would else be pointed out to no purpose. Ellicott finds here the primitive idea of the priest, not a member of a sacerdotal caste ministering to an outer world but a superior officer in a society consisting of nothing but priests, and thinks it striking how much power the presbytery already has in this earliest writing.

Barnes and Robertson agree that the three participles describe not different orders of ministers but different parts of the work the same men perform. Ellicott takes for their work's sake to mean not only because they do the work but in order to help it forward. Clarke turns it at once into maintenance, since men delight to serve those they love, and says ministers must want neither the necessaries nor the conveniences of life, adding that those who do not work should not eat. Wesley ends his note with the same sting, asking how we are to esteem them who do not work at all, and breaks out against the man who undertakes the whole work without gifts or graces and sells his own soul and the souls of the flock for pay. On the charge to be at peace Calvin prefers the old translator's reading, found also in Erasmus and Wycliffe, and judges that Paul had in view the artifices of Satan, who never ceases to stir up quarrels between people and pastor, so that pastors are daily hated by their Churches for some trivial reason or for none. Robertson puts it in a sentence: an army of captains and colonels never won a battle.

Who is addressed next is disputed. Barnes says the exhortation is evidently to the whole church and not to the ministers only, and blames the notion that admonition belongs to the officers alone for much coldness in the churches; Ellicott says flatly that the writers turn to the presbytery, and says the same of the charge about rendering evil. The vocabulary is military. Clarke works the figure through: the unruly are out of their ranks, the feeble-minded dispirited on the eve of battle by the number of the enemy, the weak wings to be shored up lest they break, and the officer who cannot reduce his troops to discipline must not lose his temper. Robertson identifies the disorderly with the market-place idlers used against Paul at Thessalonica. Calvin insists that remedies must be adapted to diseases, so the obstinate are reproved sharply and refused the soothing they demand, that the weak may be treated with kindness; and he reads the long-suffering as aimed at our irksomeness, since a man who has comforted the fainthearted twice feels at the third call a vexation that will not let him persevere. Ellicott adds that among Greeks, whose feuds were frequent and undying, abstinence from revenge was practically a new thought, and that there is not one standard of morals towards the brethren and another towards the world. Gill and Henry keep the duty mutual.
16:
The three commands are read as one chain. Calvin refers the joy to moderation of spirit, the mind keeping itself calm under adversity, and says that in recommending constant prayer Paul points out the way of rejoicing perpetually, since by this means we ask alleviation in all our distresses. Henry puts the same links plainly: the way to rejoice evermore is to pray without ceasing, we should rejoice more if we prayed more, and the meaning is not that men should do nothing but pray but that nothing else should hinder prayer in its season. Ellicott quotes an old comment to the same effect, that he who has accustomed himself to hold converse with God and to give thanks over everything as happening well will have unbroken joy, and adds that though a man cannot pray incessantly in words, the mind may be held in an attitude of prayer. He states it at its sharpest: the Christian who remains in sadness really breaks a commandment, since in some direction he mistrusts God. Wesley calls the three together Christian perfection, beyond which we cannot go and short of which we need not stop. Clarke notes that four manuscripts of good note add in the Lord.

On the thanksgiving Barnes supplies an example rather than an argument, recalling that Chrysostom, driven from Constantinople into exile and dying far from every comfort, kept repeating his motto, glory to God for all things. Ellicott will not let the clause about the will of God be read as enforcing a duty: it encourages them to see that thankfulness is always possible, since God has no wish to give them cause for sorrow but wills to fill them with thankfulness. Clarke grounds it on the promise that all things work together for good, so that prosperity and adversity are equally helpful. Calvin adds the limitation from the other side, that many pray so as to murmur against God and fret if he does not immediately gratify them, whereas we may lawfully ask and even lament, provided the will of God is more acceptable to us than our own. Wesley presses it further, that such a man neither chooses nor refuses, likes nor dislikes anything, but as it agrees with that perfect will.

Chrysostom's figure for quenching is the fullest. God has kindled a bright lamp in our souls; some have made it brighter and some have put it out; and a lamp is extinguished by throwing water or dust on it, or simply by taking out the oil, so that earthly cares quench the Spirit as surely as wickedness. He then presses it: the eye and ear are the lamp's opening and the mouth its door, and when a man insults you, opening your mouth adds force to the wind, whereas if two doors stand opposite and you shut one there is no draught and the blast is spent. What exactly is quenched divides them. Gill takes the graces, faith, love, zeal and knowledge, which cannot be utterly lost but may be greatly damped. Robertson takes the special gifts, warning of two extremes, cold indifference and wild excess. Clarke denies that the miraculous gifts can be meant, since these were given to few and even apostles could not work them at will, while the direction here is general; he adds that fire is quenched by heaping earth on it as well as by water, so the love of the world quenches the Spirit as effectually as any transgression. Ellicott warns against taking the word too sharply of the Person, who may be grieved or neglected but never extinguished, and closes with a quotation: Christianity is an enthusiasm, or it is nothing. Calvin distinguishes general from particular, quenching being the wider fault and despising prophecy a species of it. Barnes makes it a matter of culture: a man has no more religion than he intends to.
20:
Nearly all take prophesying to mean preaching. Calvin says expressly that he understands not the gift of foretelling the future but the science of interpreting Scripture, so that a prophet is an interpreter of the will of God and prophecy is interpretation made suitable to present use; he then turns the verse against fanatics who despise the ministry of man and Scripture itself in order to attain the Spirit, and set forth as secret revelations whatever is breathed into their ears. His conclusion is that we must conjoin the Spirit with the voice of men, which is nothing else than his organ, and let heaven and earth be commingled rather than that prophecy should cease. Wesley says the same in a line: the apostle is not speaking of extraordinary gifts. Barnes suspects that at Thessalonica, as later at Corinth, speaking in unknown tongues was rated far above the plain statement of religious truth. Ellicott lays out three explanations and prefers his own: their despondency made them turn a cold ear to the prophets, which quenched the Spirit in the prophets too. He rejects the view that they were dazzled by showier gifts, since nothing proves it and their fault was not sensationalism but a tendency to damp all ardour alike. Robertson defines the word as forth-telling rather than fore-telling; Gill alone extends it to the written prophecies.

On proving, Barnes takes the word from the assayer, whose trial was by fire, and builds on it his largest claim: Christianity does not ask men to receive as undoubted truth all that synods and councils have decreed, and is more than any other religion the friend of free inquiry; we are to examine every opinion, no matter by whom held or by what antiquity sustained, and then hold what we have found true though it cost a martyr's death. Calvin comes at it from the other side, that many are almost disgusted with the very name of prophecy because so many blab out worthless contrivances from the pulpit and some babble blasphemies, yet judgment must precede rejection; and he infers that the spirit of discrimination is conferred on believers, since otherwise the command to prove would have been given in vain. Ellicott adds that the word rendered good here is not the moral term used a few verses earlier but means genuine, answering to what a thing purports to be. Clarke would have the teachers themselves tried by the word of God, observing that even then men professed to be of God and were not. Cyril turns the same clause into a rule of church membership: make thy fold with the sheep, flee the wolves, depart not from the Church, learn to distinguish the pastures of doctrine, and be an approved banker, holding fast that which is good.

The last clause divides them. Gill, Barnes and Clarke read it of the appearance of evil, Barnes drawing a rule for doubtful cases and Clarke warning against driving morality so near the bounds of evil that weak persons believe we touch it. Ellicott says flatly that this translation cannot stand, and renders it, hold yourselves aloof from every evil kind of whatever you are testing. Robertson agrees that the papyri support the sense of class or kind, though the word naturally means look or appearance, and denies that it would mean semblance as opposed to reality. Calvin rejects both the universal reading and the one making it a subdivision of a general term, calling the latter an exceedingly gross blunder, and takes it of doctrine in which falsity is not proved but a suspicion is left that some poison lurks; from such we are to suspend our step rather than reject it outright, lest we receive anything with a perplexed conscience. Wesley ends by warning that those who heap to themselves teachers under pretence of proving all things have no countenance from this scripture.
23:
The prayer for spirit and soul and body is the most argued verse here. Ellicott calls it the fullest and most scientific psychology in Paul, not a piling up of words: the spirit apprehends realities intuitively and survives death, while the soul takes in intellect, affections and will and belongs to the lower nature, so that where the twofold division is used the soul is reckoned with the body; and on that very point he dissents from the bishop whose name his commentary bears. Calvin makes the spirit reason and the soul the will and all the affections, and rejects the account that takes the spirit for vital motion and the soul for the renewed part, since on that reading the prayer would be absurd; his picture is the understanding as mistress, the affections in a middle place and the body obedient, so that a man is entire when he thinks, desires and does nothing but what God approves. Clarke sets out three parts: the organised body, the soul as seat of affections and appetites, and the spirit as the immortal principle without which the animal functions cannot be performed. Wesley denies the scheme: only the last two are natural constituents, the first being adventitious, a gift of God to Christians only, for the soul is either matter, and so part of the body, or not matter, and so coincides with the spirit. Robertson says the verse is not necessarily trichotomy as against dichotomy, and reads it as a prayer for the man undivided. Barnes takes the division as the popular opinion, the animal life being held in common with the creatures.

Whether the sanctification prayed for is attainable now divides them. Clarke says plainly that sanctification is not to take place in, at, or after death, and that he who can believe will find this also possible to him. Barnes answers that a prayer for perfect sanctification is no proof that it is in fact attained in this life, and Henry agrees that the best are sanctified only in part, though we should press towards it. Ellicott renders it sanctify you whole rather than wholly, the idea being that no part is left unsanctified rather than that the work is finished, and puts the preservation at the coming rather than unto it. Barnes explains why the animal nature is included: for a lion to rage or the ostrich to leave her eggs involves no guilt, they being unaccountable, whereas the same temper in a man does. Ellicott makes the caller's faithfulness a ground of confidence, since God would forfeit his character if he called and did not enable men to obey, though he can do it only while they remain willing; Calvin adds that God does not promise to be a Father for one day but adopts us to cherish us ever after. Gill and Robertson refer the whole to him who calls.

The closing requests are read as liturgy. Ellicott takes the request for prayer as a petition for remembrance in the public service, and infers from some being told to greet all, rather than all one another, that the letter went to the clergy; he traces the kiss to the Communion, and notes that the kissing of the Pax replaced it in the West only in the thirteenth century. Clarke reports a Coptic reading, greet one another, noticed by neither of the great collators. The adjuration puzzles everyone. Calvin suspects spiteful men suppressing the letter, or a mistaken prudence keeping it among a few, and says those who forbid the people to read Paul are more refractory than devils. Barnes and Clarke both turn it into an argument against Rome for withholding the Scriptures. Ellicott reports one critic taking the adjuration for the mark of a forger seeking authority, and answers with another that the constant public recitation is a splendid guarantee of the letter's integrity.
